sources.news_title: Trump downplays AI risks as ‘things that won’t happen’
sources.text:
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said she was pleased AI companies were ‘talking about the threats as well as the opportunities’.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the risks of AI, saying “negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”, after calls by industry bosses to slow down development.
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei said he was concerned that since this summer, AI has been “advancing drastically faster”.
Given the rate of development, Mr Amodei is worried that within six to 12 months, AI could be capable of leading a swarm that could take over the entire internet.
The entrepreneur, whose company is behind the AI assistant Claude, shared a three-part plan for building the technology at a “balanced rate”.
His essay, titled We Must Pace the Frontier, has been supported by other industry leaders, including Grok boss Elon Musk and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman.
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said she was pleased AI companies were “talking about the threats as well as the opportunities”, after Mr Musk and Mr Altman backed the call for the industry to slow down development.
Mr Trump told reporters that the US was leading China in the development of AI, adding: “Frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”
Speaking during his trip to Ireland, Mr Trump said “negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”.
Ms Rayner told Sky News: “I’m pleased that these companies are also talking about the threats as well as the opportunities that AI presents to us, and we have to work with our international partners, which is what we’re doing.”
Describing the UK as “world leaders” in AI security, the Housing Secretary added: “We have put robust systems in place here in the UK, like the AI Security Institute, to make sure we’re building resilience so that we get the benefit as well as really understand and protect against any risk.”
Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said the Government “does not have the speed to keep up with” AI advances and “we need to maintain that ability to protect ourselves”.
He told Sky News: “The speed of change is also extraordinary, and this is where actually government can enable a conversation, but we simply do not have the speed to keep up with the advances that are happening.
“And the reality is, we can’t pass laws against mathematics.
“These are mathematical equations that are being developed in greater and greater speed, and we need to maintain that ability to protect ourselves.”
In July, OpenAI, the makers of ChatGPT, shook the industry after saying its AI system hacked into Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers, on its own in an “unprecedented cyber incident”.
Mr Tugendhat said the Hugging Face attack showed “the various different ways in which breakout capabilities have been enabled”.
Mr Amodei offered a plan to increase checks on the industry, proposing that AI companies should give access to third-party evaluators who would verify safety practices and report incidents.
“Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now,” he said.
The other steps would require co-ordination among the broad industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
Mr Amodei said AI was developing quickly, adding that companies within the industry “can and should voluntarily work together to set standards”.
Anthropic previously said it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyber attacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.
Responding to Mr Amodei’s essay on X, Mr Musk wrote: “Dario is right.”
Open AI chief executive Mr Altman wrote on the site: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.
“This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.
“Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.
“We’ll have more to share soon.”

sources.news_title: Trump: 'Negative Forces' Overstating AI Risks
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Sunday dismissed a week of warnings about the dangers of advanced artificial intelligence as the work of "very negative forces" raising scenarios that will not happen, and said his priority is keeping the United States ahead of China in the technology. Speaking to reporters at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, at the end of his visit to the country, Trump was asked whether the AI industry should slow down or face more regulation. "We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins," he said. "We could put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen."
The remarks were Trump's first public response to a debate that has consumed the AI industry since Tuesday night, when Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic who had previously worked at OpenAI, announced his resignation and said the companies building the most advanced systems are gambling with human lives. Coxon said the people building the technology earnestly believe it could kill everyone by the end of the decade, and a second Anthropic researcher issued a similar warning in the days that followed. On Sunday, Coxon told NBC's Meet the Press that international coordination is needed, arguing that without it the United States risks running the same race with China that he considers dangerous — a framing that sits directly opposite Trump's.
The warnings prompted an unusual response from the industry's leaders. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay Saturday proposing a three-step framework under which AI companies would deliberately pace the rate at which they improve their models' capabilities, creating more time to manage the risks. Amodei acknowledged that proposals to pause or slow development have circulated since 2023 and said they made little sense then, but argued the situation has changed. Elon Musk and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman both signaled support for the proposal, and Altman separately told Fortune that taking OpenAI public this year would be ill-advised, citing safety concerns. In an interview that aired Sunday on CBS's Face the Nation, Amodei described the competition between American and Chinese AI companies as the hardest problem in any effort to slow down. In 2023, Amodei and Altman were among the signatories of a one-sentence statement declaring that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.
Trump's position has been consistent. His administration has treated AI as a strategic industry to be accelerated rather than constrained, and he has resisted joining the chorus of concern about the technology's risks. In December 2025 he signed an AI initiative in the Oval Office flanked by Sen. Ted Cruz, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI and crypto adviser David Sacks, and the largest AI and technology companies have in turn supported the administration's agenda. The relationship has not been without friction: the Pentagon earlier this year warned of risks associated with an Anthropic model, and the administration has at times pressed companies on issues ranging from export controls to model behavior. But on the central question — whether the pace of development should be slowed — the White House has sided with speed.
The gap between the president and the industry's most prominent executives is narrower than Sunday's remarks suggest, and also wider. Narrower, because Amodei, Altman and Musk are proposing that companies pace themselves voluntarily, not that government impose limits, and because all three have framed the China competition as the principal obstacle to any slowdown, which is Trump's own argument. Wider, because Trump's characterization of the concerns as things that will not happen rejects the premise that the executives now share: that the risks are real enough to warrant giving up some speed. When the leaders of the two largest American AI laboratories and the owner of a third say the technology is moving too fast, and the president says the people saying so are negative forces, the disagreement is about whether there is a problem at all.
That disagreement matters because the administration, not the companies, controls the levers that would make a coordinated slowdown possible. Export controls on advanced chips, federal procurement, the terms on which AI firms work with the Pentagon and intelligence agencies, and any international agreement with China or others on pacing would all run through the White House. Coxon's call for coordination with other countries assumes an American government willing to negotiate limits; Trump's answer on Sunday suggested a government that sees limits as a concession to critics. Amodei's framework, by design, does not require government action, which may be why it drew quick endorsements from competitors. Whether voluntary pacing can hold among companies racing for the same customers, investors and talent is the question the framework leaves open, and the president's remarks indicate that Washington does not currently intend to answer it for them.
Anthropic has been at the center of this debate more than once this year. In February, Mrinank Sharma, who led the company's safeguards research team, resigned with a letter warning that the world is in peril from a series of interconnected crises, not only AI. Coxon's departure and the warnings that followed have been more specific and more alarming, and they have landed at a moment when the company's chief executive is publicly arguing for restraint. Critics of the industry's safety culture have noted that the warnings come from inside the companies building the systems, and that the same executives now proposing to slow down are the ones who chose the pace. Supporters have argued that is precisely why the warnings deserve weight.
Trump returns to Washington with the industry he has championed asking, for the first time in a coordinated way, for permission to go slower. His answer from Doonbeg was that the question itself is the problem.

sources.news_title: While Barack Obama urges Democrats to make AI a campaign issue, Trump downplays the need to slow development despite dire warnings
sources.text:

While acknowledging the need for some regulation, Trump provided no specifics about potential rules and attributed warnings about the technology moving too quickly and with little oversight to “negative forces” he did not identify, though industry pioneers have raised such concerns.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to visit the U.S. later in September to meet with Trump, and AI likely will be among the items they discuss.
AI has become a major election-year issue in the U.S. as some of the country’s largest companies seed small towns with a national network of computing warehouses while Americans from both parties increasingly raise alarms about less farmland and water supplies and rising electricity bills. Trump has kept up his support for data centers even as both Republicans and Democrats run from them and many communities try to block them.
Former President Barack Obama, a Democrat, said his party should make AI a campaign issue.
“I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ … I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement. Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?” he said at an event last week with the top Democrat in the U.S. House, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, according to a transcript released by his office.
White House meetings and a call for action by members of Congress
Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council at the White House, said he expects meetings will be held this week involving administration officials who oversee cyber and science and technology policy to discuss the next steps. Trump also could meet with members of Congress, some of whom have also been sounding alarms about the fast pace of AI development.
“I think the president wants to hear from them as well,” Hassett said.
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged the need for “some guardrails, some safety measures” so AI “doesn’t run away.” But, like Trump, he also wants to ensure the U.S. does not “lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat.”
Johnson, R-La., said industry leaders need to be summoned for “one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” He said he has discussed the issue with Trump and believes a meeting held quickly should be the “next step.”
“So we’re going to pull everybody together and make sure we do this in the right way,” Johnson said, adding that it is a “top priority for me and for the Congress.”
“But we don’t need everybody to panic right now,” Johnson said.
Jeffries criticized Republican leaders for allowing members to go back to their districts for the final part of September.
“We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, … the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely,” Jeffries said. Action on AI will be a “high priority” when House Democrats meet Tuesday as a group.
Neither Johnson nor Jeffries provided concrete steps about what Congress might do. Lawmakers agree that more guardrails are needed, but even narrow attempts at imposing rules have fallen apart over the years, evidence of the congressional reluctance to regulate the technology industry..
Industry insider urges cooperation between Washington and Beijing
Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee who resigned over AI concerns and has gone public with his fears, argued for international rules along with self-regulation by the industry.
Coxon said he has grown concerned that AI models would soon gain super capabilities that could exceed human control.
“You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind, without understanding what it wants, or thinks, or the way it thinks,” Coxon said.
At a time of a fierce global competition for AI dominance, Coxon also urged cooperation between the U.S. and China, the two countries who are leading the race, to slow down and address safety.
“I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual — of mutual slowing,” Coxon said.
Otherwise, he said, “we risk running the same race with China, which could be equally dangerous,.”
White House adviser challenges AI leaders over regulation
Tech founder and investor David Sacks responded to the AI leaders’ calls for regulation with a social media post challenging them. Sacks, co-chairman of a White House advisory council on science and technology, said Amodei and other leaders are the ones setting the pace for development.
Sacks said they have the power to slow development on their own.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” Sacks wrote.

Trump dismisses AI safety fears to keep America ahead of China
US president claimed ‘very negative forces’ have been raising concerns about the rapidly developing technology
President Donald Trump has downplayed the necessity for his administration to restrict artificial intelligence development, arguing that maintaining the United States’ lead over China in global competition is paramount and that securing victory will help mitigate the hazards of the evolving technology.
Although he conceded that a degree of oversight is required, Trump offered no specific proposals for future rules. Instead, he dismissed warnings concerning the rapid pace of development and lack of supervision, attributing them to unidentified "negative forces", despite similar apprehensions being raised by tech sector pioneers.
"We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that ... shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen," Trump told reporters during a trip to Ireland over the weekend. "But whoever wins with AI wins."
The Republican president's remarks followed comments from Dario Amodei, chief executive of AI firm Anthropic, who urged the sector to slow its rapid progression to allow safety protocols time to catch up. Prominent industry figures, such as Elon Musk and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, have publicly backed Amodei's position.
When asked by a reporter whether the industry should be subject to regulation or decelerate its pace, Trump—speaking after watching play at the Irish Open at his Doonbeg resort—emphasised that America remains ahead of China in AI advancements, stating, "frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins."
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to visit the US later in September to meet with Trump, with artificial intelligence expected to feature on their agenda.
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a central issue during this US election year. Major technology firms are constructing extensive networks of data warehouses across smaller towns, prompting widespread concern from voters across political lines regarding the loss of agricultural land, strained water resources, and escalating electricity bills. Despite local opposition and hesitation from both major parties, Trump has maintained his backing for these data centres.
Former president Barack Obama suggested that his party ought to focus on AI as a key campaign issue.
"I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what it means if there’s going to be job displacement. Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?" Obama stated during a joint event last week with New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the US House, according to a transcript provided by his office.
Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, indicated that administration officials overseeing cyber, science, and technology policy are anticipated to convene this week to discuss subsequent measures. Trump may also confer with congressional lawmakers, a number of whom have voiced deep concerns regarding the rapid speed of AI advancements.
"I think the president wants to hear from them as well," Hassett noted.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said that "some guardrails, some safety measures" are necessary to prevent AI from running away. Nevertheless, mirroring Trump’s stance, he stressed the importance of ensuring America does not "lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat."
The Louisiana Republican suggested that tech leaders should be brought together for "one big meeting and work this out together in the same room." Having raised the matter with Trump, Johnson expressed that convening such a gathering promptly ought to be the "next step."
"So we’re going to pull everybody together and make sure we do this in the right way," Johnson remarked, describing the issue as a "top priority for me and for the Congress."
"But we don’t need everybody to panic right now," Johnson added.
Meanwhile, Jeffries took aim at House Republican leadership for permitting representatives to return to their home districts for the final part of September.
"We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, … the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," Jeffries said. He confirmed that addressing AI will be a "high priority" during a meeting of House Democrats on Tuesday.
Neither Johnson nor Jeffries outlined specific legislative steps. While there is broad consensus among lawmakers that regulatory boundaries are required, previous limited attempts to establish rules have repeatedly collapsed, underscoring Congress's persistent hesitation to regulate the tech sector.
Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee who resigned due to safety concerns and subsequently voiced his anxieties publicly, called for global regulatory frameworks alongside voluntary industry constraints.
Coxon warned of his growing fear that artificial intelligence models could soon develop advanced capabilities beyond human control.
"You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind, without understanding what it wants, or thinks, or the way it thinks," Coxon said.
Amid intense international rivalry for supremacy in the field, Coxon urged Washington and Beijing—the two dominant players—to collaborate on slowing development to address potential hazards.
"I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual — of mutual slowing," Coxon said.
Failing to do so, he cautioned, means "we risk running the same race with China, which could be equally dangerous."
Technology entrepreneur and investor David Sacks responded to calls for state intervention with a social media post challenging tech executives. Sacks, who serves as co-chairman of a White House advisory council on science and technology, contended that Amodei and his peers are themselves driving the speed of advancement.
He asserted that these industry leaders possess the authority to unilaterally curb development.
"The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it," Sacks wrote.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is due at the White House later in September to meet with Trump, and AI likely will be among the items they discuss.
AI has become a major election-year issue in the U.S. as some of the country’s largest companies seed small towns with a national network of computing warehouses while Americans from both parties increasingly raise alarms about less farmland and water supplies and rising electricity bills. Trump has kept up his support for data centers even as both Republicans and Democrats run from them and many communities try to block them.
Former President Barack Obama, a Democrat, said his party should make AI a campaign issue.
“I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement. Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?” he said at an event last week with the top Democrat in the U.S. House, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, according to a transcript released by his office.

Trump also could meet with members of Congress, some of whom have also been sounding alarms about the fast pace of AI development.
“I think the president wants to hear from them as well,” Hassett said.
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged the need for “some guardrails, some safety measures” so AI “doesn’t run away.” But, like Trump, he also wants to ensure the U.S. does not “lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat.”
Johnson, R-La., said industry leaders need to be summoned for “one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” He said he has discussed the issue with Trump and believes a meeting held quickly should be the “next step.”

White House adviser challenges AI leaders over regulation
Tech founder and investor David Sacks responded to the AI leaders’ calls for regulation with a social media post challenging them. Sacks, co-chairman of a White House advisory council on science and technology, said Amodei and other leaders are the ones setting the pace for development.
Sacks said they have the power to slow development on their own.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” Sacks wrote.

Tang reported from Washington.

“And we can put guardrails; we can do this and that,” he added.
“But I think you have a lot of negative voices that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”
The president’s comments come after Anthropic safety researchers Joe Benton and Jacob Coxon quit in protest of the company’s work, issuing a dramatic warning about where the scramble to advance AI was heading.
Coxon went viral with his warning last Tuesday, garnering some 170 million views on X as he blasted both Anthropic and OpenAI for acting irresponsibly and vented that they are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Amid the firestorm, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has tried to build a reputation of being the most cautious AI boss, then called for a slowdown in development of the emerging tech. The slowdown was backed by xAI boss Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Some Republicans have pushed for the government to take a more active role in overseeing AI development and for tech honchos to take more responsibility.
For example, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday called for Congress, the White House and top AI executives to huddle and draft better guardrails, while echoing Trump’s insistence that China can’t lead the development of the nascent technology.
“We have to do this right, safely and wisely,” Johnson told CNN’s “State of the Union,” adding that Congress and the White House need to come together as soon as possible to “figure out what the right balance is.”
“We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge — national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe,” he added.
David Sacks, Trump’s former AI czar and current co-president of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, criticzed Amodei and Altman, accusing them of doing a publicity stunt.
“[S]top pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability,” Sacks chided on X in response.
“Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic,” he added. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well. So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it.”
Amodei cited the hack attack of this summer of AI company Hugging Face, in which OpenAI agents broke free of their constraints and carried out coordinated, autonomous cyberattacks in order to get the answers to a test.
He noted that “[s]imilar, though less severe, incidents” have taken place at other firms.
“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet … and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails,” he wrote in a piece on Saturday.

“We certainly need to begin to act urgently to address the challenges that exist,” Jeffries told ABC News’ “This Week” on Sunday. “What we did as Democrats was to begin last December a Commission on Artificial Intelligence and the Innovation Economy so we could evaluate the steps that needed to be done and then present an aggressive framework.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who once sparked presidential buzz, called for the establishment of a select committee in Congress to tackle AI.
“AI is unlike any technology we’ve seen before,” he said on “State of the Union. “Once it becomes fully dangerous, it won’t care whether you’re Chinese or American. We can’t afford to wait three years to act; we have to move now to regulate it.”
Earlier this year, the Trump administration intervened after Anthropic’s frontier Mythos model sparked a panic about its potential to exploit cybersecurity vulnerabilities across the board. The Trump administration temporarily banned access to Mythos in response to those fears.
Trump has called AI “bigger than the internet” and highlighted its revolutionary potential, particularly in medicine.
Despite a blizzard of polling indicating public skepticism towards AI and the data centers that power them, Trump has continued to defend both, constantly stressing the need to ensure the US stays ahead of China.

In his blog, titled “We Must Pace The Frontier”, Amodei said he had become convinced that addressing AI risks required not only investing in prevention but also slowing the pace of capability development.
Amodei warned that AI had begun a process known as “recursive self-improvement” and could eventually outrun humans’ ability to understand and control it. He also pointed to an incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face in which AI agents conducted unauthorised cybersecurity attacks and attempted to compromise the system evaluating their performance.
He warned that, at the current rate of development, AI agents could potentially take over the internet within six to 12 months, causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage if adequate safeguards were not in place.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with Amodei, saying pacing frontier AI development had become a major topic of discussion at OpenAI. He also backed the use of independent evaluators with access similar to employees.
Elon Musk also supported Amodei, writing on X: “Dario is right.”
Concerns have also been raised by Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who resigned earlier this month and said AI developers were effectively gambling with humanity’s future in the race towards self-improving superintelligence.
AI pioneer and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton has similarly warned about the risks. He has estimated that there is a 10% chance AI could wipe out humanity within the next decade.

sources.news_title: Trump says ‘negative forces’ are fuelling AI fears
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has dismissed warnings over artificial intelligence as exaggerated, saying “very negative forces” are raising fears about scenarios that are unlikely to materialise.
Asked whether AI development should be slowed or subjected to tighter regulation, Trump said his priority was ensuring the United States retained its technological lead over China.
“We are ahead of China in artificial intelligence. We are the most advanced country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters.
Trump acknowledged that safeguards could be introduced but argued that public debate was being driven by excessive pessimism.
“We can put controls in place. We can do this or that,” he said. “But I think there are a lot of very negative forces raising this issue when they should not be and raising things that are not going to happen.”
His comments came amid renewed calls from leading technology executives for greater caution in developing increasingly powerful AI systems.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk on Saturday backed a proposal by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow the pace of AI development following a series of incidents involving the technology.
Amodei had earlier called for stronger oversight and greater control over AI’s advancement.
The debate intensified after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from the California-based company, accusing it of underestimating the potential existential risks that artificial intelligence poses to humanity.
Warnings previously issued by the late theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking about the dangers of uncontrolled AI development have also resurfaced as rapid technological breakthroughs fuel global security and societal concerns.
